title: September Dawn
full_review:
Dramatically, "September Dawn" (Black Diamond) is basically your standard Western but it's decked out with a provocative theme, to be sure.

The love story of Mormon boy Jonathan (Trent Ford) and pioneer girl Emily (Tamara Hope) unfolds against a backdrop of the Mountain Meadows Massacre of Sept. 11, 1857.
This was when 120 men, women and children from Arkansas were slaughtered as their wagon train journeyed to California.

The film begins with Capt. Alexander Fancher (Shaun Johnston) stopping the train in Utah. The group needs to rest before continuing their arduous journey, but a Mormon vigilante group, led by John D. Lee (Jon Gries), approaches them menacingly and orders Fancher to move on.

But Jacob Samuelson (a fictional Mormon elder played by Jon Voight) intercedes and allows the travelers to stay for a couple of weeks, but later instructs son Jonathan to spy on them. The boy -- who impresses Fancher when he tames one of the latter's wildest stallions with ease -- catches the admiring eye of pretty Emily, and it's clear that, despite their religious differences (the Mormons disparage nonbelievers as "Gentiles"), romance is in the air.

Jonathan has shown a more tolerant spirit than his Mormon brethren, rejecting his father's enthusiastic injunction to take three or four wives, prompting his more rigidly indoctrinated brother Micah (Taylor Handley) to shadow Jonathan's every move and report what he observes to their father.

Samuelson goes to Cedar City for guidance. There, Territorial Governor (and church president) Brigham Young (Terence Stamp), fearing interference in his area by federal forces, views these strangers as interlopers who may have had a hand in the Missouri persecution of Mormons a decade earlier that resulted in the killing of prophet Joseph Smith.

Samuelson -- shown, like Young himself, to be quite hardhearted -- returns home with a clear mission: to wipe out the party, using the Paiute Indians as allies. Voight attempts some shading, and occasionally telegraphs flickers of conscience but he can only go so far with a recitation of grace capped with "May these children of Satan go to hell. Amen."
Jonathan -- who is planning to flee with Emily -- tries vainly to stop the slaughter.

Historical verification of what actually happened is sketchy, but it would appear the entire party was tricked into thinking there was a truce and, except for the children under 10, was subsequently wiped out by Indians, Mormons, or Mormons disguised as Indians. The film relied primarily on the confession of Lee, who took the fall for the massacre. (His execution is re-created.)

The Romeo and Juliet framework, understandably fashioned by director and co-writer Chris Cain (with Carole Whang Schutter) to give the story an emotional peg, is bothersome by its fictitious nature. And actingwise, Ford and Hope -- though appealing -- are disconcertingly contemporary.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has officially denied that Young actually ordered the killings, and said that, in fact, he tried to send word that the wagon train be allowed to pass. Whatever the truth, the film can at least be viewed, in generalized terms, as a warning against religious fanaticism of any stripe, a theme with great resonance in today's world.

The film contains much violence during the slaughter, shots of dead and wounded, polygamy, a brief sexual reference and fratricide. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
